prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We investigate the plasma flow properties inside a Supergranular (SG) cell, in particular its interaction with small scale magnetic field structures. The SG cell has been identified using the magnetic network (CaII wing brightness) as proxy, applying the Two-Level Structure Tracking (TST) to high spatial, spectral and temporal resolution observations obtained by IBIS. The full 3D velocity vector field for the SG has been reconstructed at two different photospheric heights. In order to strengthen our findings, we also computed the mean radial flow of the SG by means of cork tracing. We also studied the behaviour of the horizontal and Line of Sight plasma flow cospatial with cluster of bright CaII structures of magnetic origin to better understand the interaction between photospheric convection and small scale magnetic features. The SG cell we investigated seems to be organized with an almost radial flow from its centre to the border. The large scale divergence structure is probably created by a compact region of constant up-flow close to the cell centre. On the edge of the SG, isolated regions of strong convergent flow are nearby or cospatial with extended clusters of bright CaII wing features forming the knots of the magnetic network.

outputs.L1:
We investigate the plasma-flow properties within a supergranular (SG) cell, with particular emphasis on its interaction with small-scale magnetic-field structures. The SG cell was identified using the magnetic network, traced by Ca II wing brightness, as a proxy and applying Two-Level Structure Tracking (TST) to high spatial, spectral, and temporal resolution observations obtained with IBIS. The full three-dimensional velocity-vector field of the SG was reconstructed at two different photospheric heights. To strengthen our findings, we also computed the mean radial flow of the SG through cork tracing.

We further examined the behaviour of the horizontal and line-of-sight plasma flows co-spatial with clusters of bright Ca II structures of magnetic origin, in order to better understand the interaction between photospheric convection and small-scale magnetic features. The SG cell investigated here appears to be organized by an almost radial flow extending from its centre to its boundary. The large-scale divergence structure is likely produced by a compact region of persistent upflow near the cell centre. At the edge of the SG, isolated regions of strong convergent flow are located near, or are co-spatial with, extended clusters of bright Ca II wing features that form the knots of the magnetic network.

We examine the characteristics of plasma motions within a supergranular (SG) cell, with special attention to how these flows interact with small-scale magnetic structures. The SG cell was detected by using the magnetic network, traced through Ca II wing brightness, as an indicator and by applying Two-Level Structure Tracking (TST) to IBIS observations with high spatial, spectral, and temporal resolution. The complete three-dimensional velocity field of the SG was derived at two distinct heights in the photosphere.

To make our results more robust, we additionally estimated the average radial flow of the SG through cork-tracing techniques. We also analyzed the horizontal and line-of-sight plasma motions located in the same areas as clusters of bright Ca II features of magnetic origin, aiming to clarify how photospheric convection interacts with small-scale magnetic elements.

The SG cell under study appears to exhibit a nearly radial flow pattern, directed from the center toward the boundary. Its large-scale divergent structure is likely produced by a compact zone of persistent upflow near the middle of the cell. Along the SG perimeter, separated areas of intense converging motion are found close to, or spatially coincident with, extended groups of bright Ca II wing structures that constitute the knots of the magnetic network.
outputs.L3:
The study investigates the plasma flow properties within a Supergranular cell and explores how these flows interact with small-scale magnetic field structures. In particular, it focuses on the organization of photospheric motions inside the cell and on the relationship between these motions and the magnetic network that outlines the cell boundaries.

The Supergranular cell was identified using the brightness of magnetic network features observed in the Ca II wing as a proxy for the cell boundary. These bright Ca II wing structures trace concentrations of magnetic field and therefore provide a useful diagnostic for locating the magnetic network surrounding the Supergranular cell. The analysis was carried out using high-resolution observations obtained with the Interferometric BIdimensional Spectrometer (IBIS). To characterize the dynamics of the observed region, the data were processed with the Two-Level Structure Tracking method, which allows the horizontal proper motions of photospheric structures to be measured with high spatial and temporal detail.

From these observations, the full three-dimensional velocity vector field of the Supergranular cell was reconstructed at two different heights in the photosphere. This made it possible to examine how the flow pattern changes with height and to obtain a more complete description of the plasma dynamics within the cell. In addition, the mean radial flow was independently estimated through cork-tracing techniques, in which passive tracers are advected by the measured velocity field to reveal the large-scale transport pattern.

The results show that the investigated Supergranular cell is largely organized by an almost radial outflow. Plasma appears to move from the central region of the cell toward its periphery, forming a coherent large-scale horizontal flow pattern. This outward motion is consistent with the typical behavior expected in Supergranulation, where material rises near the cell center, spreads horizontally across the photosphere, and converges near the network boundaries.

Near the edge of the cell, the analysis reveals strong convergent flows. These convergence zones are found close to, or aligned with, clusters of bright Ca II wing features. Such bright clusters correspond to knots of the magnetic network, where small-scale magnetic field elements accumulate. The spatial association between converging plasma flows and magnetic network knots suggests that the Supergranular flow plays an important role in transporting and concentrating magnetic elements at the cell boundaries. Thus, the observed velocity field provides evidence for a direct interaction between the large-scale Supergranular flow and the small-scale magnetic structures that define the magnetic network.

The study examines the plasma flow pattern inside a solar supergranular cell and its interaction with small-scale magnetic structures in the photosphere and low chromosphere. The supergranular cell is identified using the brightness distribution observed in the wings of the Ca II line, where enhanced emission outlines the magnetic network surrounding the cell. High-resolution observations obtained with the Interferometric BIdimensional Spectrometer (IBIS) are analyzed in order to derive the horizontal motions of photospheric structures. To do this, the study applies the Two-Level Structure Tracking technique, which follows the displacement of intensity structures at different spatial scales and provides detailed maps of the horizontal velocity field.

From these measurements, the authors reconstruct the three-dimensional velocity field associated with the supergranular cell. The results show that the cell is characterized by a nearly radial horizontal outflow extending from its central region toward its boundaries. This outward motion appears to be driven by a central up-flow, consistent with the classical picture of supergranulation as a convective pattern in which plasma rises near the center of the cell, spreads horizontally across the photosphere, and then converges and sinks near the cell edges.

To better understand how this flow affects the magnetic elements, the study also uses cork tracing. In this method, passive tracers are placed in the measured velocity field and allowed to move with the plasma flow. The corks progressively accumulate at the boundaries of the supergranular cell, where the horizontal flows converge. These convergence regions coincide with bright Ca II knots associated with the magnetic network, indicating that the plasma motions sweep small-scale magnetic elements toward the cell edges and concentrate them there.

Overall, the study demonstrates that photospheric convection plays a key role in organizing small-scale magnetic structures on the Sun. The supergranular flow transports magnetic elements from the cell interior toward the network boundaries, where they accumulate in regions of strong convergence and enhanced Ca II brightness. This provides a clear observational link between the dynamics of convective plasma flows and the spatial distribution of magnetic features in the solar atmosphere.
outputs.L5:
**The Supergranular Network in Ca II Observations**

The supergranular pattern is one of the most important large-scale flow structures observed on the surface of the Sun. Supergranules are convection cells much larger than ordinary granules, typically measuring about 20,000 to 30,000 kilometers across. They are produced by plasma motions beneath the solar photosphere and play a major role in organizing magnetic fields on the solar surface.

The Ca II spectral lines, especially the Ca II H and Ca II K lines, are widely used to study the Sun’s chromosphere. In Ca II images, the boundaries of supergranular cells often appear as bright network structures. This happens because magnetic fields are swept by horizontal plasma flows toward the edges of supergranules, where they become concentrated. These magnetic concentrations heat the chromospheric plasma, making the network brighter in Ca II emission.

Observations of the supergranular network in Ca II are valuable for understanding solar magnetism, chromospheric heating, and the connection between surface flows and the upper solar atmosphere. The Ca II lines reveal details that are not always visible in white-light images, allowing scientists to trace how magnetic fields evolve over time.

In summary, the supergranular pattern and the Ca II emission network are closely linked. The study of supergranular structures in Ca II provides important insight into the dynamic behavior of the Sun and the processes that shape its atmosphere.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a solar physics paper about plasma flows inside a supergranular cell observed with IBIS, using Ca II wing brightness, TST tracking, 3D velocity reconstruction at two photospheric heights, cork tracing, and magnetic network interactions.
counterfactuals.output: We present high-resolution IBIS observations of plasma flows inside a quiet-Sun supergranular cell, using Ca II wing intensity as a proxy for photospheric brightness structure. Horizontal motions were derived through time-series tracking (TST) of intensity features, while line-of-sight Doppler signals were combined with the tracked proper motions to reconstruct the three-dimensional velocity field at two photospheric heights. Cork advection was used to visualize long-term transport and identify preferred convergence sites. The resulting flow maps reveal persistent outward motions from the cell interior toward the magnetic network, with height-dependent changes in speed and topology. Cork accumulation occurs preferentially near network boundaries and localized magnetic concentrations, indicating efficient transport of plasma and small-scale magnetic elements toward the supergranular edges. Interactions between the reconstructed flows and the magnetic network suggest that network geometry modulates convergence, shear, and downflow locations. These results demonstrate the diagnostic value of combining Ca II wing imaging, feature tracking, 3D velocity reconstruction, and cork tracing for characterizing mass transport and magnetic coupling in the photospheric supergranular pattern.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the findings of a study investigating the interaction between photospheric convection and small-scale magnetic structures in a supergranular cell, including radial outflows, central upflows, and convergent flows near Ca II bright magnetic network knots.
counterfactuals.output:
The study found that the small-scale magnetic field in a supergranular cell is strongly organized by the photospheric convective flow field.

- **Central upflows and divergent motion:**  
  The interior of the supergranular cell showed broad, weak **upflows** in the photosphere. These upflows fed a largely horizontal, **radially outward flow** from the cell center toward the cell boundary.

- **Radial transport of magnetic elements:**  
  Small magnetic flux concentrations in the cell interior were passively advected by these outward granular/supergranular flows. As a result, internetwork magnetic elements tended to migrate from the cell center toward the magnetic network at the cell edges.

- **Network formation and concentration:**  
  At the supergranular boundary, the outward flows from neighboring regions converged, collecting magnetic flux into stronger, longer-lived magnetic concentrations. These concentrations appeared as **bright Ca II network knots**, indicating enhanced chromospheric emission above strong photospheric magnetic fields.

- **Convergent flows near Ca II bright knots:**  
  Around the Ca II bright magnetic network knots, the flow pattern changed from divergence to **convergence**. Plasma motions were directed toward the magnetic concentrations, often associated with localized downflows. This suggests that network magnetic knots are rooted in intergranular/downflow lanes where convective collapse and flux concentration can occur.

- **Magnetic–convective coupling:**  
  The observations showed a close interaction between convection and magnetic structure: convection transports and concentrates magnetic flux, while strong magnetic concentrations locally modify the convective flow pattern.

Overall, the study concluded that a supergranular cell is characterized by **central photospheric upflow, radial horizontal outflow, and converging/downflowing motions at the magnetic network boundaries**, where Ca II bright knots mark concentrated magnetic flux.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an academic-style paragraph describing how a supergranular cell was identified through CaII wing brightness, analyzed with Two-Level Structure Tracking, and used to reconstruct horizontal and line-of-sight plasma flows.
counterfactuals.output: A supergranular cell was identified from the enhanced brightness pattern observed in the Ca II line wing, where the chromospheric/network emission delineated the cell boundaries and provided a proxy for the underlying magnetic network. The selected cell was then analyzed using the Two-Level Structure Tracking (TST) technique, which follows the apparent displacement of intensity structures at two hierarchical spatial scales in order to infer the horizontal transport field across the solar surface. By applying TST to the Ca II wing image sequence, the horizontal plasma velocities were reconstructed, revealing the characteristic divergent flow from the cell interior toward the network lanes. Complementary line-of-sight velocities were obtained from spectral diagnostics, allowing the Doppler component of the plasma motion to be mapped across the same field of view. Together, the TST-derived horizontal motions and the line-of-sight velocity field provided a three-dimensional description of the supergranular flow pattern, linking the bright Ca II wing network boundaries to the converging downflow regions and the cell interior to weaker, outward-directed horizontal motions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a research abstract on high-resolution IBIS observations of a supergranular cell, focusing on 3D velocity fields, cork-traced radial flows, and the relationship between plasma flow patterns and bright CaII magnetic features.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

We present high-resolution imaging spectropolarimetric observations of a quiet-Sun supergranular cell obtained with the Interferometric Bidimensional Spectrometer (IBIS), aimed at characterizing the three-dimensional plasma velocity field and its relationship to chromospheric magnetic structuring. Line-of-sight velocities were derived from photospheric and chromospheric spectral diagnostics, while horizontal proper motions were inferred through local correlation tracking of granulation and visualized using passive cork advection. The resulting flow maps reveal a coherent, large-scale radial outflow from the interior of the supergranular cell toward its network boundaries, with horizontal velocities organized into persistent divergence patterns and localized convergence lanes. Cork trajectories trace the progressive evacuation of cell interiors and accumulation of tracers along the supergranular boundary, consistent with the advection of magnetic flux by convective motions.

The reconstructed 3D velocity field shows that photospheric horizontal flows dominate the transport pattern, while line-of-sight velocities display smaller-scale upflow and downflow patches associated with granular and intergranular dynamics. Near the cell boundary, enhanced convergence coincides with stronger downflow signatures and with the concentration of bright Ca II features, interpreted as magnetic network and plage-like elements. These Ca II brightenings are preferentially located where corks accumulate, indicating that the magnetic field is passively swept toward supergranular boundaries by radial plasma motions and subsequently intensified in converging flow regions. In contrast, the cell interior is characterized by weaker Ca II emission, reduced magnetic structuring, and persistent divergent horizontal flows.

Our results demonstrate the diagnostic power of IBIS for linking photospheric velocity fields to chromospheric magnetic emission at high spatial and temporal resolution. The observed spatial correspondence between cork-traced convergence zones, downflowing plasma, and bright Ca II magnetic features supports a scenario in which supergranular flows regulate the distribution and evolution of small-scale magnetic fields. These observations provide quantitative constraints on the coupling between convection-driven transport, magnetic flux concentration, and chromospheric heating in quiet-Sun network regions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a scientific summary of a solar observation study where TST is applied to CaII wing images to examine supergranular plasma flow organization and its interaction with small-scale magnetic field structures.
counterfactuals.output:
A solar observation study applied the **Two-Dimensional Correlation Tracking Technique (TST)** to a time series of **Ca II wing filtergrams** in order to investigate how horizontal photospheric plasma flows are organized on **supergranular scales** and how those flows interact with small-scale magnetic magnetic elements.

The observations sampled the lower solar atmosphere in the wings of the Ca II line, where intensity structures can be used as tracers of photospheric motions. By tracking the apparent displacement of these fine-scale brightness features over time, TST produced two-dimensional horizontal velocity maps. These maps revealed a coherent large-scale flow pattern characteristic of **supergranulation**: plasma diverged outward from cell interiors and converged toward the cell boundaries. The inferred flow field showed organized meso- to supergranular circulation rather than purely random granular motions.

When compared with contemporaneous small-scale magnetic structures, the velocity maps indicated that magnetic elements are strongly shaped by the plasma flow. Weak magnetic flux concentrations were transported by the horizontal motions, swept out of supergranular cell interiors, and accumulated along converging network lanes. In these boundary regions, the interaction between converging flows and magnetic features led to clustering, intensification, and persistent organization of the magnetic network.

The study therefore demonstrated that TST applied to Ca II wing images is an effective method for diagnosing horizontal photospheric flow fields. It showed that supergranular plasma motions play a central role in redistributing small-scale magnetic flux, maintaining the magnetic network, and coupling convective dynamics to magnetic structuring in the lower solar atmosphere.
